proofs.full_local_argument: Fix arbitrary mu,b>0. For h(a)=mu*a^2/2, h'(a)=mu*a, h*=0 and argmin h={0}. Consequently (1/2)|h'(a)|^2=mu^2*a^2/2=mu(h(a)-h*), so PL holds for all a. QG with gamma=4mu would require mu*a^2/2 >= 2mu*a^2. For every a!=0 the left side is one quarter of the right side, so the displayed inequality is not satisfied for this example. Next complete the square: h_theta(a)=mu*(a-b*theta/mu)^2/2-b^2*theta^2/(2mu). Its unique minimum is attained at a*=b*theta/mu, its minimum value is -b^2*theta^2/(2mu), and h_theta'(a)=mu*(a-b*theta/mu). Therefore (1/2)|h_theta'(a)|^2=mu(h_theta(a)-min h_theta) for every theta,a. In particular the PL-game condition holds uniformly, and A(theta)={b*theta/mu} is a closed singleton. For smoothness, partial_theta f=b*a and partial_a f=b*theta-mu*a. Thus variation of partial_theta f with theta is zero; variation of partial_a f with a has magnitude mu*|a1-a2|; variation of partial_a f with theta has magnitude b*|theta1-theta2|; and variation of partial_theta f with a has magnitude b*|a1-a2|. These prove Assumption 2.5 with L11=0,L22=mu,L12=b; increasing L11 to b^2/(4mu)>0 preserves the assumption. For any distinct theta1,theta2, the only possible maximizers satisfy |a*(theta1)-a*(theta2)|=(b/mu)|theta1-theta2|>b|theta1-theta2|/(2mu). The selected example therefore has the coefficient b/mu; the coefficient in A.3 is not adopted for this example. Substituting a* into f gives g(theta)=b^2*theta^2/(2mu), so g'(theta)=b^2*theta/mu=partial_theta f(theta,a*(theta)). For every distinct pair, |g'(theta1)-g'(theta2)|/|theta1-theta2|=b^2/mu. Thus the exact Lipschitz constant is b^2/mu, strictly larger than the printed b^2/(2mu), or 3b^2/(4mu) under the positive alternative L11. All assumptions used in this diagnostic have now been checked explicitly; no source lemma or external theorem is needed to obtain these explicit constant comparisons.

printed_claims: Lemma A.2 prints QG gamma=4mu under the displayed PL convention.
Lemma A.3 prints the existential argmax selection bound L12/(2mu), with a closed argmax set.
Lemma A.5 prints L=L11+L12^2/(2mu) under Assumption 2.5 and the PL-game assumption.

assumptions: mu>0 and b>0 are arbitrary real parameters; inner maximization is over all R.
Choose the valid block smoothness constants L11=0, L22=mu and L12=b in Assumption 2.5. If strictly positive L11 is desired, L11=b^2/(4mu) is also valid and still yields the counterexample.
Theta=[-1,1] is convex, compact and contained in the radius-one ball. The function is the restriction of a polynomial on R^2, so derivatives at boundary points are defined by that extension.
statement.conclusion: The function h is mu-PL with equality and has minimum 0 at a=0, but fails QG with gamma=4mu. For every theta, h_theta is mu-PL with equality and A(theta)={b*theta/mu} is nonempty and closed. Thus |a*(theta1)-a*(theta2)|=(b/mu)|theta1-theta2|, whereas Lemma A.3 Eq.(15) with L12=b displays coefficient b/(2mu), which is not adopted for this example. Moreover g(theta)=b^2*theta^2/(2mu), g'(theta)=b^2*theta/mu, and its exact gradient Lipschitz constant on [-1,1] is b^2/mu. This exceeds Lemma A.5's printed L11+L12^2/(2mu)=b^2/(2mu) for L11=0, and also exceeds 3b^2/(4mu) for the positive admissible alternative L11=b^2/(4mu). The marginal gradient identity itself holds in this example.
statement.objects_and_definitions: Use scalar real variables and absolute-value norms. Set h(a)=mu*a^2/2 on R. On Theta=[-1,1], A=R, set f(theta,a)=b*theta*a-mu*a^2/2; define h_theta(a)=-f(theta,a), A(theta)=argmax_a f(theta,a), and g(theta)=max_a f(theta,a). PL means (1/2)|h'|^2 >= mu(h-h*); QG means h-h* >= (gamma/2)dist(a,argmin h)^2.
statement.parameter_domains: mu,b in (0,infinity); a in R; theta in [-1,1]. No asymptotic limit or randomness.
statement.quantifiers_and_randomness: For every mu>0 and b>0 the following deterministic conclusions hold. The QG failure holds for every a!=0. The sensitivity and marginal smoothness failures hold for every pair of distinct theta1,theta2 in [-1,1]; the unique maximizers leave no alternative selection that could satisfy the smaller bound.
